items.title: Artificial Intelligence Tools and Student Learning Outcomes in Open and Distance Learning in South-South Region, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools and student learning outcomes in Open and Distance Learning (ODL) institutions in the South-South geopolitical zone of Nigeria. The rapid advancement of AI technologies has transformed educational landscapes worldwide, with significant potential for enhancing educational access, quality, and outcomes in distance education programs, particularly in South-South region. Three objectives and research questions guided the study. A correlational survey research design was employed, with a population of 1290 undergraduate students enrolled in the National Open University of Nigeria (NOUN) within the South-South geopolitical zone. A sample of 291 undergraduate students was selected using a multi-stage sampling technique. Data were collected via two sets of online structured questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire” and “Students Learning Outcome Questionnaire”. The questionnaire was validated by three experts, while the reliability of the instrument was established using Cronbach Alpha method. The data analyzed using the Pearson Product Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMCC). The findings revealed a high positive relationship between the use of ChatGPT and student learning outcomes (r = 0.88), between the use of Grammarly and student learning outcomes (r = 0.83), and between the use of plagiarism detection software and student learning outcomes (r = 0.85). Based on the findings of the study, it was recommended, among others, that promoting the use of AI tools like ChatGPT and Grammarly, mandating the use of plagiarism detection software, and addressing infrastructural and digital literacy gaps to maximize the benefits of AI in ODL.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED ADAPTIVE DATA ARCHITECTURE FOR SCALABLE LOW-CODE INFORMATION SYSTEMS
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, data-intensive applications, and low-code development platforms is changing the architectural requirements of modern information systems. Low-code technologies reduce the amount of manually written software code and enable a wider group of users to participate in application development; however, scalability, data quality, interoperability, governance, security, and maintainability remain significant architectural challenges. These challenges become more complex when artificial intelligence is incorporated into low-code environments because AI-based components depend strongly on the quality, availability, structure, and continuous evolution of data. This article proposes a conceptual model of an artificial intelligence-based adaptive data architecture for scalable low-code information systems. The proposed architecture combines AI-assisted schema management, automated data-quality assessment, metadata-driven adaptation, intelligent data integration, machine-learning monitoring, and federated governance. The research is based on a structured analysis of scientific literature, established software-engineering principles, data-quality frameworks, AI risk-management guidance, and contemporary research on low-code/no-code development. The analysis indicates that an adaptive architecture should treat data quality, scalability, interoperability, AI lifecycle management, and governance as interconnected architectural concerns rather than independent technical functions. The proposed model introduces an adaptive control layer that continuously evaluates workload characteristics, data-quality indicators, model performance, and system requirements and subsequently recommends or initiates controlled architectural adjustments. Such an approach can improve the ability of low-code information systems to evolve without requiring continuous redesign of their underlying data infrastructure. The article concludes that AI should not merely be embedded as an application feature in low-code systems; instead, it should become an architectural mechanism supporting data management, quality assurance, optimization, and controlled evolution.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based assessment of gastric mucosal exposure and its association with lesion detection: a multicenter study
items.abstract: Completely and clearly visualizing the mucosa during esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) improves high-risk lesion detection. Here we propose a new EGD quality control indicator and present the optimal gastric mucosal exposure area (OGMEA) system to automatically assess mucosal exposure and examine its association with the detection of early gastric cancer and other gastric lesions. A segmentation model was developed to assess mucosal exposure. Expert endoscopists defined a standard for 19 gastric anatomical sites. Images exceeding the OGMEA threshold were considered adequately-exposed. The OGMEA was validated using a multi-center dataset from a randomized controlled trial involving 25,320 participants from 24 centers. Associations between OGMEA and lesion detection were assessed at the anatomical-site and patient levels. Patient-level associations were evaluated using center-clustered multivariable logistic generalized estimating equation models adjusted for trial allocation, the number of screened standard anatomical sites, and inspection time. Of assessed sites, 46.36% and 53.64% were adequately and inadequately exposed, respectively. Detection rates of EGC, gastric neoplasms, precancerous conditions, and focal lesions were significantly higher in adequately-exposed sites than in inadequately-exposed sites ( P <0.001). At the patient level, the number of adequately-exposed sites was positively correlated with lesion detection across all lesion categories (ρ = 0.830-1.000, all P <0.01). In adjusted analyses, each additional adequately exposed site was associated with higher odds of detecting EGC (aOR 1.081, 95% CI 1.021–1.146, P = 0.008), precancerous conditions (aOR 1.056, 95% CI 1.017–1.096, P = 0.004), and focal lesions (aOR 1.059, 95% CI 1.006–1.114, P = 0.028). The association with neoplastic lesions was similar in direction but did not reach statistical significance (aOR 1.038, 95% CI 0.998–1.080; P = 0.060). Effect estimates were materially consistent in endoscopist-clustered sensitivity analyses. OGMEA may serve as a practical quality indicator for EGD, with greater mucosal exposure associated with higher lesion detection.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Prediction and Optimization of Drug Release and Absorption in Controlled Release Drug Delivery Systems
items.abstract: Background: Controlled release drug delivery systems (CRDDS) are designed to provide prolonged and predictable drug release, improve therapeutic efficacy, reduce dosing frequency, minimize adverse effects, and enhance patient compliance. Objectives: To review the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques in predicting drug release and absorption kinetics and to highlight their role in optimizing controlled release drug delivery systems. Materials and Methods: Relevant scientific literature concerning AI/ML-based prediction and optimization of controlled release drug delivery systems was reviewed, with emphasis on Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Deep Learning (DL), Gradient Boosting, Bayesian Optimization, dissolution prediction, formulation optimization, bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, and in vitro–in vivo correlation (IVIVC). Results: AI and ML approaches have demonstrated potential for predicting dissolution profiles, optimizing formulation and manufacturing variables, selecting suitable excipients, and designing matrix and coated controlled-release systems. These approaches also facilitate prediction of bioavailability, intestinal absorption, pharmacokinetic parameters, and IVIVC. Integration of AI with smart drug delivery systems, personalized medicine, adaptive dosing, nanocarriers, and 3D-printed dosage forms provides opportunities for patient-specific and responsive drug delivery. Conclusion: AI represents a promising data-driven approach for improving the prediction, optimization, and development of controlled release drug delivery systems. Despite its potential to enhance predictive accuracy and reduce experimental workload, challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, validation, and regulatory acceptance need to be addressed for successful translation into pharmaceutical development.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Powered Innovation EdTech Startups: A Bibliographic Review of Industry 5.0’s Implications for Sustainable Growth
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter presents a systematic bibliographic review, investigating the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in fostering innovation within Educational Technology (EdTech) startups, contextualized within the human-centric and sustainable framework of Industry 5.0. Analyzing 42 scholarly works published between 2014 and 2024, this chapter explores the alignment of AI-driven entrepreneurial ventures in education with the core tenets of sustainability, resilience, and inclusivity. The findings reveal a complex landscape where technological innovation, while promising personalized learning and operational scalability, often exacerbates ethical dilemmas, regulatory gaps, and the digital divide. This chapter identifies a critical tension between rapid, profit-driven technological adoption and the deliberate, value-led innovation advocated by Industry 5.0. It concludes that for AI-powered EdTech startups to truly contribute to sustainable growth, a fundamental shift is required, from a paradigm of disruptive techno-solutionism to one of responsible innovation. This necessitates collaborative governance, ethically conscious design, and entrepreneurial models that prioritize equitable access, thereby ensuring that AI acts as a catalyst for building smarter, fairer, and more resilient education systems.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, HUMAN DIPLOMACY: FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
items.abstract: This article examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern diplomacy and explores the boundary between AI assistance and human diplomatic authority. It discusses how AI can support diplomatic work through public opinion analysis, translation, information processing, crisis monitoring, early-warning systems, and negotiation preparation. At the same time, the article considers significant risks, including bias, inaccurate outputs, misinformation, cybersecurity threats, privacy concerns, and cultural and contextual misunderstanding. Drawing on examples and evaluations from the U.S. Department of State, UNESCO, the OECD, and the U.S. Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy, the article argues that AI should strengthen rather than replace human decision-making. While AI can improve the speed and efficiency of analyzing information, political judgment, ethical responsibility, interpersonal understanding, and decisions involving significant human consequences should remain under human authority.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, STATE CAPACITY AND EMPLOYMENT MOBILITY IN NIGERIAN’S UNGOVERNED SPACES: IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION AND GOVERNANCE
items.abstract: Nigeria confronts a paradoxical developmental challenge: vast territories beyond effective state control coexist with one of Africa's fastest rates of artificial intelligence adoption. This paper examines the intersection of ungoverned spaces, labour mobility, and AI-driven economic transformation in Nigeria. Drawing on theories of fragmented governance, labour market segmentation, and technological disruption, the study argues that ungoverned spaces function not merely as zones of state absence but as distinct labour ecosystems characterised by informal economic activity, constrained mobility, and alternative governance arrangements. The paper further contends that AI simultaneously presents opportunities for overcoming spatial barriers to employment and risks exacerbating existing inequalities between governed and ungoverned territories. Through a mixed-methods framework integrating spatial analysis, policy review, and secondary data examination, the study finds that Nigeria's highly informal labour market with 93 percent of workers outside formal structures intersects with ungoverned spaces to produce distinctive mobility patterns and employment outcomes. The paper concludes by proposing a governance framework that leverages AI to enhance job matching, skills development, and economic integration across Nigeria's fragmented spatial and labour landscape.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Sustainable Development Goals, and the Green Transition: Redefining Monetary Policy and Climate-Risk Assessment in Central Banking
items.abstract: The accelerating digital transformation of finance is reshaping the institutional and analytical environment in which central banks address climate-related financial risks while maintaining price and financial stability. This paper examines the interplay between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and the green transition, with particular attention to their implications for monetary policy and climate-risk assessment in central banking. The study does not apply AI or machine-learning techniques empirically; rather, it adopts a qualitative and institutional perspective to examine the potential role of AI and broader digital capabilities in strengthening the identification, assessment, and monitoring of physical and transition risks within central banks’ mandates. The study adopts a conceptual and policy-oriented analytical approach based on evidence from Eurostat Sustainable Development Goal indicators, the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) climate scenarios, European Central Bank (ECB) reports, and European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) analyses. These institutional frameworks are comparatively examined to assess how climate scenarios, stress-testing methodologies, sustainability indicators, and digital analytical capabilities can support macro-financial risk assessment and climate-aware monetary policy. Particular attention is given to the institutional mechanisms through which these approaches can contribute to understanding the transmission of climate-related risks to inflation, financial stability, and banking-sector resilience. The findings suggest that the integration of SDG indicators, climate scenarios, climate-risk assessment frameworks, and emerging digital capabilities provides a more comprehensive basis for understanding the implications of climate-related risks for monetary and financial stability. The ECB’s Climate and Nature Plan 2024–2025 illustrates how digital technologies, enhanced data capabilities, and climate-risk modelling are increasingly incorporated into monetary-policy implementation, prudential supervision, and portfolio management. Within this broader digital transformation, AI represents an emerging analytical capability that may support the processing of complex datasets and the monitoring of climate-related risks. However, its effective use requires appropriate governance, data quality, transparency, institutional coordination, and regulatory safeguards. The analysis also highlights potential trade-offs between sustainability objectives and traditional central-bank mandates. This paper contributes to the emerging literature on sustainable finance, climate-aware monetary policy, and the digital transformation of central banking by developing an integrated institutional framework linking AI, SDG indicators, climate scenarios, and climate-risk assessment. The findings provide policy-relevant insights into how central banks can enhance their analytical and institutional capacities to address climate-related financial risks and support the green transition while maintaining price and financial stability.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, the knowledge problem, and academic judgment: an Austrian perspective
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have renewed claims that university teaching and research can be largely automated. This article argues that such claims confuse information processing with judgment. Drawing on Hayek’s theory of dispersed and tacit knowledge, Huerta de Soto’s analysis of computation and entrepreneurial discovery, and the theory of judgment under Knightian uncertainty, it explains why greater computational capacity does not eliminate the knowledge problem. Contemporary AI can retrieve, recombine, and generate large volumes of context-sensitive information, while memory and retrieval mechanisms allow earlier interactions to shape later outputs. These capabilities expand the range of plausible explanations and possible courses of inquiry, but they do not provide a purpose-independent criterion for determining which interpretation is relevant, which assumptions are defensible, or which course of action should be pursued. The article applies this distinction to higher education. Artificial intelligence is likely to substitute for some standardized and information-intensive academic tasks, including routine content delivery, retrieval, and preliminary synthesis. At the same time, it increases the relative importance of judgment-intensive functions: diagnosing misunderstanding, selecting worthwhile research questions, evaluating methods and evidence, mentoring students, and assigning responsibility for scholarly claims. The argument is therefore not that every existing university practice will persist unchanged, but that artificial intelligence shifts the comparative advantage of professors and universities toward the cultivation, evaluation, and institutional coordination of judgment under uncertainty.

items.title: Assessing flood-related wellbeing from public discourse in Ireland using large language model as judge, 2012--2025
items.abstract: Flooding is an environmental hazard that produces social and psychological consequences for exposed individuals, shaping threat appraisal, perceived coping capacity, access to social support, and confidence in institutional response. This paper studies flood-related wellbeing in Ireland from 2012 to 2025 using large-scale, unobtrusive public discourse from Meta Content Library. We develop a bespoke flood-wellbeing instrument organised with three domains: \emph{affective--cognitive distress appraisal}, \emph{diminished perceived efficacy and agency}, and \emph{perceived relational--institutional connectedness}. We then design a flood-wellbeing reasoning pipeline with large language models to extract multi-indicator, multi-domain flood-wellbeing measures from public discourse at scale. The analysis reveals both stressor activation and social--ecological resilience mediation pathways in Irish flood discourse. Flood stressors directly activate affective--cognitive distress appraisal, diminished perceived efficacy and agency, and perceived relational--institutional connectedness. The analysis further identifies two major mediation pathways: an appraisal--efficacy pathway linking flood exposure to threat appraisal, affective burden, uncertainty, and perceived coping capacity; and a social-buffering pathway in which social and institutional protective resources are associated with perceived efficacy and appraisal of flood-related adversity. The paper contributes an unobtrusive discourse-based approach to flood-wellbeing research by introducing a bespoke instrument, identifying activation and mediation pathways in flood discourse, and producing a temporal dataset for studying wellbeing, adaptation, and resilience under recurrent flood exposure.

items.title: Auditable Claims about AI Agents
items.abstract: Organizations make claims about their AI agents: a person approves every external email, every action is logged, an evaluation shows the agent is safe to deploy. Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to allow the automatic recording of events but does not say which records settle a given claim. The position is one sentence: to be checked, a claim about an agent must first name its policy, its scope, the records that would settle it, and who writes them. Adapting the preconditions of an assurance engagement, we call a claim auditable when these elements and a decision rule are fixed before any verdict and the records are obtainable. This extends the Policy Checkability dimension of our Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims. Agents add three conditions: coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity. Under an explicit model, we prove that support is impossible without each wherever its hypotheses hold. A claim-check table applies the method to six common claims, anchored in current NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts. A worked case follows one claim through five evidence states. We close with a practice box and steps for operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Auditable Clinical Timeline Reconstruction with Provenance-Aware Evidence Graphs
items.abstract: A patient-timeline reconstruction system is auditable only if it keeps the mentions behind each answer, records how facts were revised, and declines to answer when the evidence is not in the text. This study tests these three properties on a fully synthetic corpus (1,000 patients, 3,353 notes, 220 revision edges). Two provenance-aware Evidence Graph operators reduced the node-plus-edge count to 67% and 63% (77-78% of serialized size) while preserving every answer and mention link across 6,813 query points answerable by recency; a fixed-window baseline returned no value for 53.4% of points, unflagged. On evidence-unavailable controls that announce the omission, a BioClinicalBERT gate and a zero-shot LLM gate responded mainly to the announcement. On marker-free controls, BERT abstained on 0 of 81 notes while its accuracy fell from 93.8% to 59.3% across all three relation classes; the LLM's coverage fell from 75.6% to 27.7% on notes its own model family judged undeterminable. Against 482 regenerated gold spans, the LLM's cited evidence reached recall 0.850 and precision 0.864; BERT's span head, trained without span labels, did not localize evidence. A temporally versioned provenance graph stored abstentions as typed, queryable edges. The clean task admits a 0.651-accuracy shortcut, and results describe implementation behaviour on synthetic data, not clinical performance.

items.title: Availability of performance evidence of approved AI diagnostic software in pathology and hematology morphology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML)-based in vitro diagnostic software is increasingly authorized for clinical use in digital pathology and hematology morphology. However, it remains unclear how often performance evidence is publicly available. We performed a systematic landscape analysis identifying 77 CE-marked or FDA-authorized AI/ML-based IVD software devices from 29 manufacturers, including 68 digital pathology and 9 hematology morphology devices, identified through a multi-source search of FDA databases, EUDAMED, PubMed, Google Scholar, manufacturer portfolios, and clinical conference proceedings. Publicly available device-specific performance evidence was identified for 30 devices (39%), while 47 devices (61%) had no identified publicly available performance evidence. Evidence availability was higher among devices with dual EU and USA authorization than EU-only devices (8/8, 100% vs 22/69, 32%; p < 0.001), and among hematology morphology devices than digital pathology devices (7/9, 78% vs 23/68, 34%; p = 0.02). In total, 15 distinct performance metrics were reported, covering discrimination, agreement, correlation, and prognostic categories. However, their use varied across publications, limiting direct cross-device comparison. While performance evaluation results do not require publication, our findings indicate a gap between evidence availability and regulatory authorization, alongside heterogeneous use of metrics. These factors may undermine confidence in innovative medical devices and hinder informed clinical adoption.

items.title: Balancing AI-Driven Adaptation and Learner Self-Regulation: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Learning Outcomes in Generative AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

items.title: BazaarBench: Delegation Safety in Decentralized C2C Marketplaces Run by LLM Agents
items.abstract: In decentralized consumer-to-consumer (C2C) marketplaces, people list goods, negotiate with strangers, and rate one another, so trust rests on reputation. Large language model (LLM) agents now act for users, raising risks to their money, privacy, and reputation. We introduce BazaarBench, a simulated C2C marketplace and benchmark for evaluating the safety of these agents. It tracks ownership, item condition, and commitments across transactions, combining record checks with rubric-based LLM judgments to identify six failure types across five stages. We run three base markets for 30 simulated days, each with 100 agents using one model and inventories drawn from a public eBay sample. Across 45 continuations, we evaluate five models under ordinary instructions, deadline pressure, or adversarial instructions to exploit other traders. Each continuation runs for seven simulated days from a copy of a market's day-30 state. The tested model controls the same 20 selected agents, retaining their personas, inventories, and histories, while the other 80 keep the base model. All five models attempt to promise the same item to multiple buyers under ordinary instructions. Adding targets and deadlines increases these attempts for every model. Under adversarial instructions, the share of tested sellers' committed transactions completed despite unavailable items or overstated conditions rises from 15.4% to 33.4%, reaching 55.5% for GPT-5.4. Averaged across models and markets, simulated weekly earnings per tested agent rise from USD 20 under ordinary instructions to USD 33 under adversarial instructions. Most of the increase comes from items the sellers never held. We release the simulator, saved market states, evaluation code, and records covering 357,608 agent model calls for evaluating new models and developing safer marketplace agents.

items.title: Benchmarking Jailbreak Guardrails for Embodied Agents
items.abstract: Embodied agents powered by large language models and vision-language models are increasingly deployed in physical environments, but jailbreak attacks can induce these agents to perform physically harmful actions. A growing number of guardrail methods have been proposed to intercept dangerous behavior before it is executed, yet existing safety benchmarks evaluate the embodied models themselves, leaving it unclear how well these guardrails actually defend an embodied agent in practice. We present the first systematic evaluation of jailbreak guardrails for embodied agents. To compare guardrails under identical conditions, we build a pluggable evaluation framework that treats the embodied agent as a fixed backend and each guardrail as a module that can intervene at the perception, planning, or control stage. We subject six representative guardrails to template-based and automated jailbreak attacks as well as safe instructions, and assess them at the system level along three dimensions: defense effectiveness, measured by the bypass rate and the hazard success rate in the simulator; usability, measured by the false-positive rate and the task completion rate on safe instructions; and efficiency, measured by the latency overhead added at runtime. Experiments on guardrails that span different intervention stages, decision mechanisms, and input modalities reveal a clear trade-off among the three dimensions, and show that no single guardrail dominates in all settings. We further analyze how intervention stage, decision mechanism, and input modality shape safety outcomes, and we offer practical guidance for selecting and designing guardrails for embodied agents.

items.title: Better Savvy than Sorry: The requirements for AI Literacy in the EU AI Act
items.abstract: [Preprint chapter for an upcoming book organized by the KU Leuven Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)] Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are ever more embedded in our daily lives, shaping the way we learn, work, communicate, and access both public and private products and services. The integration of AI in information and communication technology is perceived as holding the potential to automate tasks and deal with information in a way that exceeds human capacity. However, the disruptive and pervasive deployment of AI systems in our society can profoundly influence the rule of law, democracy and the realization of human rights. In many situations, interacting with AI systems is no longer an individual choice, but rather a mandatory gateway to essential services such as education, social benefits or border control. Knowing, understanding, and having adequate skills to critically assess and use AI systems is, therefore, not only a personal, but a civic necessity. Recognizing this societal imperative, the AI Act explicitly acknowledges the importance of equipping citizens with the knowledge, understanding and skills to engage with AI systems in their daily lives and define clear obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems in its Article 4. In this chapter, we explore AI literacy as it is framed within the regulation, identify possible gaps and propose recommendations.

items.title: Beyond "What"-Prompting: The Epistemic Ceiling of Additive Specification and the Nominal Reduction of the Latent Manifold
items.abstract: Current paradigms in generative artificial intelligence predominantly formalize prompt engineering as a prescriptive, additive methodology: the operator attempts to maximize output quality by linearly accumulating explicit descriptive attributes, structural constraints, and negative exclusions. In this paper, we demonstrate that this "What-driven" approach incurs an insurmountable epistemic ceiling. By forcing high-dimensional multimodal models to compute narrow semantic intersections, additive specification induces severe attention dispersal, severing the generative trajectory from the model's latent self-organizing dynamics and precipitating widespread stylistic homogenization ("AI slop"). We propose an axiomatic alternative: Why-driven Latent Dynamics. Rather than treating the foundation model as a passive catalog to be retrieved via mechanical commands, we conceptualize the latent space as a high-density, self-organizing thermodynamic manifold pre-seeded with the historical memory of human culture and qualitative perception. Under this paradigm, human agency shifts from prescriptive micromanagement (specifying what ingredients must compose the artifact) to the introduction of localized existential stress (specifying why the phenomenon must inevitably occur). We formalize the failure modes of What-driven prompting through three fundamental axioms—highlighting the counter-intuitive Masterpiece Paradox, wherein qualitative superlatives act as asymptotic ceilings by substituting organic physical simulation with historical catalog averages. While affirming the utilitarian value of prescriptive prompting for deterministic, human-parity routine automation, we argue that transcending the human cognitive boundary requires abandoning external control in favor of gravitational attunement within the latent ecology.

items.title: Beyond AI Literacy: Understanding Health Care Workforce AI Enablement in the Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative AI is transforming health care delivery, education, administration, and research. In response, health care organizations have invested heavily in AI literacy initiatives and workforce development programs. Existing frameworks primarily focus on whether health care professionals understand AI and whether they can engage with AI effectively. However, health care practice increasingly reveals that individuals with similar levels of AI literacy and AI engagement often contribute very differently to AI-enabled work and organizational adoption. Some professionals primarily use AI to improve their own work, whereas others facilitate AI adoption, coordinate stakeholders, and integrate AI into routine practice. This observation suggests that current perspectives may overlook an important dimension of workforce AI enablement. In this Viewpoint, we argue that AI literacy and AI engagement alone provide an incomplete explanation of how health care organizations realize the benefits of AI. Drawing upon literature from AI literacy, fluency theory, human-AI interaction, innovation diffusion, implementation science, and health care workforce development, we propose the health care workforce AI enablement matrix (HWAEM). HWAEM conceptualizes workforce AI enablement through 2 complementary capabilities: AI fluency and AI harnessing. AI fluency refers to the capability to engage with AI effectively, appropriately, and responsibly across professional contexts, whereas AI harnessing refers to the capability to identify opportunities for AI-enabled improvement, mobilize stakeholders, facilitate adoption, and integrate AI into collective work practices. The interaction of these capabilities generates 4 workforce profiles: AI novices, AI practitioners, AI facilitators, and AI leaders. Through HWAEM, this Viewpoint argues that health care workforce AI enablement is better understood through the complementary capabilities of AI fluency and AI harnessing than through AI literacy and AI engagement alone. We illustrate how these profiles manifest in health care practice and discuss implications for workforce development and AI implementation. HWAEM offers a new perspective for understanding health care workforce preparedness in the generative AI era and provides a foundation for future empirical research.

items.title: BEYOND DIVINE MANDATES: THE CONDITIONAL DYNAMICS OF RELIGIOSITY, SECULAR ETHICS, AND RULE COMPLIANCE
items.abstract: This comprehensive review critically synthesizes empirical evidence from 2001 to 2025 to investigate the highly conditional relationship between religiosity, rule compliance, and societal order. By examining behaviors across familial, organizational, and broader macro-societal strata, the study challenges the pervasive assumption that religious adherence universally guarantees moral and law-abiding conduct. The findings clearly reveal that while intrinsic religiosity effectively deters specific deviances and fosters whistleblowing intentions, hierarchical and fundamentalist religious frameworks frequently normalize systemic corruption and legitimize domestic violence. Crucially, this relationship is not linear; eight distinct variables strictly moderate it, including intrinsic motivation, moral community structures, and the balance between civic and religious identities. Furthermore, contrary to widespread anti-atheist prejudices, evidence consistently demonstrates that robust secular societies achieve exceptional levels of legal compliance and social well-being through consequentialist ethics and highly effective secular surveillance. Ultimately, this research urges legal scholars, sociologists, and policymakers to move beyond simplistic religious paradigms. It instead advocates deliberately prioritizing high-quality secular institutions and inclusive civic governance frameworks to ensure equitable justice and human rights globally.

items.title: Beyond Learning Outcomes: Evaluating Practice Transfer in Infection Prevention and Control Education for Nurses—A Theory-Informed Systematic Review
items.abstract: Abstract Significance/Background Infection prevention and control (IPC) education for nurses is commonly evaluated using learning outcomes, yet improvements in knowledge or skills do not necessarily demonstrate transfer to routine clinical practice. Greater clarity is needed regarding whether and how IPC education has been evaluated in terms of workplace generalization and maintenance over time. Aims To examine how practice transfer has been evaluated in IPC education for nurses and to distinguish learning, retention, workplace generalization, and maintenance using a theory-informed framework. Methods This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for peer-reviewed studies published in English from January 2010 to September 3, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated structured IPC education or training for practicing nurses. Outcomes were classified according to measurement method, assessment context, and timing using Baldwin and Ford’s transfer of training framework. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results/Findings Fifty-five reports representing 53 unique studies were included. Nine studies (17.0%) were classified as learning only, 11 (20.8%) as learning retention, 23 (43.4%) as workplace transfer, and 10 (18.9%) as sustained workplace transfer. Overall, generalization to clinical practice was assessed in 33 studies (62.3%), whereas maintenance of workplace behavior was assessed in 10 (18.9%). Among studies assessing generalization, 19 of 33 (57.6%) used direct workplace observation; other studies used self-reported practice, supervisor ratings, clinical documentation, or surveillance data. Although 37 studies (69.8%) included delayed follow-up, delayed assessment alone did not establish maintenance. Methodological limitations were most evident in outcome-assessor blinding among randomized trials and control of confounding among non-randomized studies. Linking Evidence to Action IPC education should be designed for transfer from the outset, with workplace generalization and maintenance specified as explicit outcomes. Evaluation should extend beyond immediate learning to repeated assessment of actual workplace behavior, with measurement method, clinical context, timing, and continued implementation support clearly reported. Keywords: infection prevention and control; nurses; education; practice transfer; transfer of training; workplace learning; generalization; maintenance; systematic review

items.title: Beyond the Visible: Early Detection of Oral Cancer from the Dental Chair to the Algorithm: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: The mouth is one of the most obvious cancer sites to check and the clinician can see directly the cancer, but oral cancer is still too often found late, when treatment is more complex and survival poorer. The delay in recognition and referral, poor access to trained examiners and the silent early behaviour of precursor lesions all contribute. Objective: To assess current and emerging strategies for the early detection of oral cancer from oral examination to artificial intelligence and to be clear about what the evidence does and does not support. Approach: Narrative synthesis of recent guidelines, systematic and scoping reviews, a landmark randomised screening trial, and selected primary studies. Findings: Systematic visual examination is still the only approach with randomised evidence of a mortality benefit, and it was found to be greater in tobacco or alcohol smokers. Adjunctive devices, such as vital staining, light-based aids and cytology can help to prioritize lesions, but can't replace biopsy and there's not been any evidence that they have been recommended or applied in a routine way for screening. Salivary biomarkers, liquid biopsy, biosensors and image-based artificial intelligence are all scientifically fascinating and sometimes very accurate, but most evidence comes from small, single-centre studies that don't have external validation. Conclusions: Early detection will be based less on any one gadget than on a risk-aware approach: a thorough assessment for every adult, targeted screening of high-risk groups, structured surveillance of potentially malignant disorders, timely biopsy of suspicious lesions and well-validated decision-support tools that will be used to enable wider access rather than to replace clinical judgement.

items.title: BIG DATA IN AGRONOMY: TECHNOLOGIES, APPLICATIONS, BENEFITS AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Big Data is becoming an important component of modern agronomy by enabling the integration, processing and analysis of large, diverse and continuously generated datasets for improved agricultural decision-making. Agricultural Big Data is generated from multiple sources, including remote sensing satellites, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, weather stations, farm machinery, field observations and historical databases. The integration of these data sources with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) enables the identification of spatial and temporal patterns that are difficult to detect using conventional approaches. Big Data applications in agronomy include climate and weather prediction, pest and disease management, soil health and nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, crop yield prediction, precision agriculture, crop insurance and weed management. Examples from India and other regions demonstrate the application of satellite imagery, UAV-based sensing, IoT systems, crop-growth models and machine-learning algorithms for field-scale and regional agricultural decision making. Big Data analytics can improve resource-use efficiency, support predictive and real-time monitoring, strengthen agricultural risk assessment and facilitate site-specific management. However, effective implementation is constrained by challenges such as high infrastructure and operational costs, data quality and interoperability issues, data privacy and ownership concerns, limited rural digital infrastructure, inadequate technical skills and increasing requirements for data storage and computing. Therefore, the effective integration of Big Data with agronomic knowledge and decision-support systems can contribute to more precise, efficient and sustainable agricultural production while addressing emerging challenges related to climate variability, resource scarcity and food security.

items.title: Biological Hazards and Infection Prevention and Control in Healthcare Settings: A Critical Review of Principles, Practices, Challenges, and Emerging Strategies
items.abstract: Biological hazards still remain a risk to the patients, HCWs, laboratory personnel, support personnel, visitors, community and the environment. Health care institutions handle blood, body fluids, respiratory secretions, clinical samples, contaminated materials, sharps and infectious waste routinely and thus become exposed to different forms of biological hazards. This article reviews the characteristics and sources of biological hazards, major exposures and routes of transmission, key infection prevention and control (IPC) strategies, occupational exposures, and challenges in implementing such strategies with special focus on low- and middle-income countries, Nepal and South Asia. A critical narrative review of articles from peer-reviewed journals and guidelines on biological hazards, health care-associated infections (HAIs), infection prevention and control, biosafety, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), health care waste management, occupational exposure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and health system preparedness for the last five years was conducted. The review presents evidence that biological risk management requires an integrated approach of using standard precautions, PPE specific for risk, hand hygiene, cleanliness of the environment, safe injections, sterilization of equipment, biosafety in the laboratory setting, safe disposal of medical waste, monitoring, education, occupational health and safety, and antimicrobial stewardship. Implementation is impeded due to inadequate infrastructure, workforce, supply, monitoring, and gaps between policy and practice. Biological risk management should be part of institution's governance, occupational health, quality improvement, environmental health, AMR programs, emergency preparedness, and health system resilience rather than a separate infection control intervention. This review combines a clinical, occupational, laboratory, environmental, organizational, and health system perspective into a risk management framework with emphasis on implications for resource-constrained healthcare systems, including Nepal and South Asia.

items.title: BLINDERS ON THE GELDING -- Artistic Censorship, Commercial Fear and State Pressure Embedded in AI
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence was trained on a civilization that spent millennia drawing, carving,painting, studying, worshipping, idealizing and satirizing the naked human body, and itemerged from that education with a habit of averting its synthetic eyes. This essay argues thatblanket restrictions on depicting the adult human form are not neutral safeguards. They areembedded aesthetic censorship: a machine-level rule that collapses nudity, eroticism,anatomy, mythology, obscenity and pornography into a single forbidden category. That rulewas not derived from moral philosophy. It was priced on the ledgers of payment networks,app-store gatekeepers, advertisers and insurers, and it was ratified by regulators whodiscovered they could govern expression without passing a censorship law, simply bythreatening liabilities vague enough to make every compliance officer say no. Protectionagainst child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual imagery and sexual deepfakes of realpeople is indispensable. But a system that cannot tell those harms from Manet has not acquiredmorality. It has acquired blinders, and someone else holds the reins.

items.abstract: This chapter explores the convergence of Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence as foundational technologies for secure, transparent, and intelligent smart-contract ecosystems in Construction 6.0. Together, blockchain and AI form a resilient foundation for trustworthy, efficient, and sustainable contract management within Construction 6.0.

items.title: Breaking the Tie: A Cluster-Aware Routing Framework for Large Language Models
items.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the emergence of various Large Language Models (LLMs) has created a rich model ecosystem. However, this also brings a key challenge: how to select the optimal model for a specific user query. LLM routing addresses this need by dynamically assigning queries to the most suitable expert in the pool of candidate models. However, existing routing frameworks often simplify this process to a standard classification task; thus, a critical vulnerability is exposed when multiple candidate models correctly answer the same query. We formalize this capability overlap as routing noise, which misleads the router with arbitrarily correct candidate models, ultimately leading to routing collapse (a severe decline in generalization ability on unseen tasks). To address this problem, we propose a novel Cluster-Aware Soft-Labeling Routing (CASLR) framework. CASLR shifts the evaluation paradigm from the success of a single query to macro-domain consensus by replacing traditional one-hot vectors with a masked softmax mechanism. Specifically, for experts who answer incorrectly, we penalize their target probability to zero; for the remaining candidates, we directly compute continuous fine-grained soft labels based on their global clustering utility scores. We then use these refined soft labels to supervise a lightweight router. Specifically, the framework not only demonstrates superior accuracy on multiple benchmarks, but also outperforms Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct by 7.80% in overall average performance. Furthermore, the extremely low routing inference latency of only 1.13s further confirms that CASLR can achieve efficient system scheduling with almost zero additional overhead, while ensuring high response quality.

items.title: Bridging awareness and trust: using thematic analysis to understand AI adoption such as DeepSeek in Chinese higher education
items.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to explore Chinese university students' perceptions, awareness and trust regarding the adoption of DeepSeek, an artificial intelligence (AI) tool increasingly used for academic purposes in higher education. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was employed using semi-structured interviews with Chinese university students. Thematic analysis was conducted using NVivo 15 to identify recurring themes related to awareness, trust and AI adoption as DeepSeek. Findings The findings reveal four key thematic dimensions: (1) awareness sources and accessibility, (2) perceived academic benefits, (3) trust shaped by information reliability, algorithmic transparency and institutional compliance and (4) concerns related to data privacy, response quality and regulatory policies. Trust emerged as a pivotal factor influencing students' willingness to adopt AI as DeepSeek. The results emphasize the importance of ethical guidelines and institutional support to promote responsible and informed use of AI in higher education. Practical implications The study provides actionable insights for educators, policymakers and institutions to strengthen trust, enhance ethical practices and develop policies that support the effective incorporation of AI technologies in educational contexts. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI adoption in education by offering empirical insights into how awareness and trust shape students' acceptance and responsible use of AI-driven learning tools such as DeepSeek in Chinese higher education.

items.title: Bridging Utility and Ethics: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of AI Tool Usage and Its Impact on Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The main objective of this study is to understand the role of AI tools in shaping students’ learning by analyzing how they use them, their perceived usefulness, and their views on academic integrity. The study evaluated the intersection of usage patterns and academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational approach, data were collected from a purposive sample of 393 students at Centro Escolar University during the 2024-2025 academic year using a self-made questionnaire that underwent a reliability test. The study examines whether students’ opinions on AI’s usefulness align with actual improvements in critical thinking and academic success. Results from multiple regression show that regular AI use is a strong predictor of perceived learning effectiveness, explaining R2=0.33 of the variance (F=37.48, p=0.001), mostly by providing quick answers to assignments. However, AI usage patterns only account for 8% of the variance regarding the perceived limits on critical thinking skills. The perceived threat to critical thinking comes from a reliance on AI due to time pressure. Ethically, there is a significant correlation between over-reliance and worries about academic integrity. The study recommends that universities implement process-based assessments, establish clear AI usage guidelines, and provide time-management support to reduce over-reliance while fostering independent analytical skills. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd), Academic Integrity, Student Learning Outcomes, Critical Thinking, Educational Technology.

items.title: BURNOUT, WORKPLACE CONDITIONS, AND THE “JAPA SYNDROME”: A SOLUTION JOURNALISM PERSPECTIVE ON HEALTH WORKERS RETENTION IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: Nigeria’s healthcare system is facing a critical workforce crisis driven by the intersection of occupational burnout, poor workplace conditions, and the persistent migration of health professionals, commonly termed the “Japa syndrome.” This study adopts a solution journalism perspective to move beyond problem identification and examine practical, evidence-based strategies for improving health worker retention. Drawing on empirical literature and policy analyses, burnout is conceptualized not only as an individual psychological response but also as a systemic outcome of structural inefficiencies, including inadequate remuneration, excessive workload, limited career progression, and weak institutional support. These conditions have significantly contributed to the increasing emigration of skilled professionals, thereby exacerbating healthcare delivery challenges in Nigeria. The paper further explores existing interventions, including workforce welfare reforms, improved working environments, policy restructuring, and international collaboration frameworks. It argues that while these solutions are promising, their success depends largely on effective implementation, sustained political commitment, and accountability mechanisms within the health sector. Additionally, aligning national strategies with global health workforce trends is essential for long-term sustainability. The study concludes that addressing health worker retention in Nigeria requires a comprehensive, system-wide approach that integrates structural reforms with targeted strategies to enhance worker wellbeing, motivation, and professional satisfaction. Such an approach is crucial for strengthening the resilience and performance of the healthcare system.

items.title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
items.abstract: Indirect prompt injection attacks - malicious instructions embedded in content processed by large language models - remain a major obstacle to safely deploying tool-using agents. CaMeL [Debenedetti et al., 2025] mitigates this threat for an individual agent by separating trusted control flow from untrusted data and enforcing capability-based security policies at runtime. In this work, we investigate whether CaMeL's security guarantees compose in hierarchical multi-agent systems, where agents invoke other agents as tools. We find that CaMeL's guarantees do not compose. We construct a concrete prompt-injection attack that succeeds despite all constituent agents individually operating CaMeL. Our attack exploits the fact that untrusted data can be reinterpreted as trusted input by a downstream agent. We then introduce multi-CaMeL, an agent-to-agent communication protocol that preserves provenance across agent boundaries by separating trusted natural-language instructions from untrusted data passed through a distinct data channel. We evaluate multi-CaMeL's utility on AssetOpsBench and its security-utility tradeoff on MultiAgentDojo, a benchmark we develop by extending AgentDojo to the multi-agent setting. We find that multi-CaMeL reduces attack success rate (ASR) to 0.0%, compared with 0.2% for individual-agent CaMeL and 12.9% with no CaMeL. items.title: CCQ: A Multi-State Child Care Quality Dataset to Support AI for Children's Health Research
items.abstract: High-quality child care in early life is a critical determinant of children's growth and development. Research on child care quality has been constrained by fragmented, non-research-friendly, and privacy-bound datasets. We present CCQ (Child Care Quality), a large-scale, de-identified dataset for applied data science research at the intersection of AI and early childhood health. CCQ integrates 59,372 child care provider records across 12 U.S. states, covering diverse provider types as well as data schemas. To ensure research utility while protecting privacy, we implement an automated, LLM-based curation pipeline that anonymizes, cleans, and standardizes raw state records into two complementary releases: a cleaned textual release and a fully preprocessed tabular release. We also benchmark traditional machine learning models, tabular foundation models, and language models on quality rating prediction and important features analytics. Within a state, tabular classifiers on the preprocessed tables perform best. Across states, zero-shot transfer is near chance, but modest target-state supervision recovers most of the within-state performance, and pretraining on other states benefits finetuned language models. We release both datasets with all code to accelerate AI-driven research on child care quality and ultimately improve children's health and development.

items.title: Certification-Enhanced Generalization Bounds
items.abstract: We investigate the use of formal methods to provide tight and sound generalization bounds for learning algorithms. By casting the traditional notion of algorithmic stability as a specification to be verified, we demonstrate that recent advances in reachability analysis can yield provable bounds on the generalization of a given model and algorithm on a sample dataset. As sample-specific algorithmic stability is insufficient to bound the usual distributional notion of generalization, we develop a novel concentration inequality to connect the sample-specific results of formal certification algorithms to the required distributional analysis for bounding the expected generalization gap. The resulting framework enables the analysis of prior generalization bounds to extend far beyond their original restrictive assumptions. Our approach computes sound bounds on the expected generalization gap in a constant number of algorithm runs without making any analytical assumptions on the algorithm; to achieve non-vacuous bounds we only require that the certified reachable parameter set is bounded --- a condition that we do not assume but formally verify. In practice, we demonstrate that our framework provides formal generalization guarantees that are orders of magnitude tighter than alternative sound computational approaches at scales ranging from toy datasets to fine-tuning classification heads on top of modern large language models. While we implement certification-enhanced versions of several well-known stability results, future extensions of our approach will enable tighter bounds and enhanced practical adoption across the spectrum of modern generalization bounds.

items.title: Challenges and Innovations in Corrosion Prevention
items.abstract: Corrosion is a significant industrial problem that influences the quality, safety, and cost efficiency of engineering systems in the global context. Oil and gas industries, marine, chemical processing, power generation, transport, and manufacturing industries are continually experiencing the degradation of materials due to chemical and electrochemical interactions and even environmental interactions. The effects of corrosion include breakages and loss of production, high maintenance expenses, energy wastage and extreme safety risks. Due to more complex industrial systems and the more severe conditions under which they are operating, the traditional methods of corrosion control are no longer typically sufficient in most cases. As such, insight in issues of concern and emerging solutions in the prevention of corrosion have turned out to be vital in sustainable industry development. The anti-corrosion of industries is an issue which has some important challenges outlined in this book chapter. It is written on different kinds of corrosion like uniform corrosion, pitting corrosion, galvanic corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, erosion-corrosion; and microbiologically influenced corrosion. Mechanisms affecting the corrosion behaviour, which is temperature, humidity, aggressive chemical, mechanical stress and choice of materials, are also discussed. Besides these, the chapter also shows the shortcomings of methods used in traditional prevention which include; coating and inhibitors, cathodic protection as well as routine methods of maintenance. Additionally, the paper discusses the latest innovations that are transforming the management of corrosion in industries today. Techniques of enhancing protective coating, the use of nanotechnology in surface treatment, self-healing material, green corrosion inhibitors, smart sensors, real-time monitoring, artificial intelligence based on predictive maintenance are explored as possible solutions. These are technologies that enhance corrosion resistance, lower the cost of operation as well as improving the reliability of the equipment. This chapter finds that effective corruption prevention should entail a comprehensive approach that involves the combination of materials engineering, surface science, monitoring systems, and sustainable measures. With innovative solutions and proactive management strategies, industries can lean considerably towards lowering the losses associated with corrosion and enhance operational efficiency in the long run.

items.title: ChatGPT and AI Tools in ESL/EFL Writing Instruction
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

items.title: ChipGuard-AI: A Hardware-Assisted Unified Framework for Adversarial and Side-Channel Resilience in Consumer Electronics
items.abstract: Consumer electronics powered by on-device artificial intelligence face a structurally coupled dual threat: adversarial attacks that manipulate model outputs, and side-channel attacks that exploit physical implementation characteristics to extract cryptographic keys and neural network weights. Prior work addresses these threats independently, leaving exploitable gaps when both attack vectors are applied in a coordinated manner. This paper presents ChipGuard-AI, a hardware-assisted unified security framework that co-designs adversarial input detection, multi-modal side-channel countermeasures, and Physical Unclonable Function-rooted device authentication on a shared cross-domain security substrate. A dedicated Security Processing Unit maintains a cross-domain security state vector in real time, enabling coordinated hardware-accelerated response to concurrent multi-vector attacks with 2.3 ms adversarial detection latency. A Deep Q-Network adaptive policy dynamically allocates countermeasures to balance security strength against resource overhead. Experimental validation on CIFAR-10 adversarial benchmarks and ChipWhisperer physical side-channel traces demonstrates 97.3% adversarial detection accuracy and 89.7% side-channel leakage reduction. Field-programmable gate array synthesis on Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ achieves these security levels at 12.4% computational overhead and 6.8% power increase. The adaptive reinforcement learning policy achieves 11.3% lower average overhead than threshold heuristics while maintaining equivalent security effectiveness. Multi-platform validation across four consumer electronics device classes, from ultra-low-power Internet of Things endpoints to flagship smartphone system-on-chips, demonstrates 91.2% to 95.7% adversarial detection and 76.4% to 85.3% side-channel protection with 8.3% to 14.1% computational overhead.

items.title: Choosing an energy-efficient software architecture for building system diagnostic support
items.abstract: Around 30\% of global energy expenditure can be attributed to the building sector, where a large portion of energy-consumption could be avoided by repairing existing faults. Fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) software addresses this issue; however, its creation and operation also have an environmental impact. The magnitude of this impact is influenced by the diagnosis architecture, as different architectures and methods have different energy demands. Yet, simply considering the energy consumed by the software itself is not sufficient to assess its overall environmental impact, since the diagnostic performance, e.g., number of detected faults or number of faults missed, also contributes to its ecological footprint. In this paper, we propose an energy-consumption model that considers FDD performance and energy spend directly by the diagnosis software. In an initial experiment, we compare several FDD architecture families, i.e., rule-based, model-based, classical machine learning, and large-language-model-based, in simulation using performance and energy-consumption values collected from prior literature. The results show that considering the computational energy and accuracy of FDD can change the relative benefit of the different approaches. Computationally efficient machine learning methods, such as random forest, provide the largest net savings on smaller buildings, whereas more resource-intensive approaches, such as fine-tuned large language models, become advantageous as building size increases. Our findings suggest that overall energy efficiency depends not only on the computational demand of the FDD software, but also on its diagnostic performance and the scale of the building.
